topStories.headline: Controller Puts a Price Tag on Prop G: Reopening Great Highway Would Cost $9.8M Up Front
topStories.dek: A new city analysis released this week says reversing the Sunset Dunes park conversion would cost nearly $10 million — intensifying the November ballot debate.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's city controller released an official cost estimate on August 11 for Proposition G, the 'Great Highway for Everyone' initiative headed to the November 3 ballot. According to the analysis, reopening the Upper Great Highway to weekday traffic would cost roughly $9.8 million upfront and up to $1.9 million annually thereafter — a figure approximately $4 million lower than estimates previously produced by the city's transportation and parks departments.

Prop G, if approved by voters, would amend the Park Code to allow cars on the two-mile stretch of the former highway between Lincoln Way and Sloat Boulevard on weekdays, while keeping Sunset Dunes Park car-free from Friday evening through Monday morning and on holidays. The road was permanently converted into Sunset Dunes Park following voter approval of Proposition K in November 2024.

The measure qualified for the November ballot after organizers submitted more than 15,626 signatures to the Department of Elections last month. Backers — including District 4 Supervisor Alan Wong and small-business owner Albert Chow — describe the proposal as a 'compromise' that would restore weekday traffic while preserving weekend park access. Opponents, including the group Friends of Sunset Dunes, counter that the measure would require the city to tear out every park feature, including picnic areas, seating, and a skate park, and would eliminate the approximately 60 percent of park visits that occur on weekdays.

Since Sunset Dunes opened in April 2025, the park has drawn more than 1.7 million visitors. The November election will mark the third time in roughly four years that San Franciscans have voted on the fate of the coastal road — a divisive issue that helped fuel the recall of former District 4 Supervisor Joel Engardio and has reshaped west-side politics.

topStories.headline: Inner Sunset Vibrancy Fund Opens Applications — With a Priority Deadline of Aug. 28
topStories.dek: A privately funded grant program from SF New Deal is offering up to $20,000 to Inner Sunset small businesses for storefront improvements and filling vacant spaces.
topStories.body:
The nonprofit SF New Deal has launched the Inner Sunset Neighborhood Vibrancy Fund, a pilot grant program backed by anonymous donors from within the neighborhood, offering financial support to new and existing small businesses along the Irving Street corridor. Applications are being accepted on a rolling basis, but priority is given to submissions received by August 28.

The fund provides grants in three categories: up to $10,000 for storefront beautification — such as replacing damaged awnings, repairing broken windows, or restoring outdoor planters — up to $5,000 for technical assistance, and up to $20,000 for businesses taking over a vacant storefront. The program is designed to support up to 20 local businesses and is geographically targeted to commercial properties between Fifth Avenue and 19th Avenue, bounded by Lincoln Way and Kirkham Street.

The initiative is the first of its kind to bring the downtown vibrancy-fund model to a residential neighborhood. SF New Deal executive director Simon Bertrang has indicated that private donors approached the organization with an interest in kick-starting the fund, and that since the launch, additional Inner Sunset residents have called in to contribute. A community advisory panel — including representatives from the Inner Sunset Park Neighbors and the Inner Sunset Merchants Association — will help guide grant decisions, though SF New Deal will make the final selections.

Businesses interested in applying can find more information and the application at sfnewdeal.org/inner-sunset.

topStories.headline: Amazing Fantasy Comics Marks 26 Years on Irving Street Under Current Owner
topStories.dek: Owner Frank McGinn's beloved Inner Sunset comic shop is being celebrated this August as it passes its 26th anniversary under his stewardship.
topStories.body:
Amazing Fantasy, the comic book shop at 650 Irving Street in the Inner Sunset, is marking 26 years under the ownership of Frank McGinn this August — a milestone highlighted in a feature in the August 17 edition of the Sunset Beacon. McGinn took possession of the storefront in August 2000, when the former Comics and Comix chain vacated the space, and neighboring Irving Street residents immediately began poking their heads in to see what was arriving.

The shop has become a cornerstone of the Inner Sunset's commercial corridor, offering back issues, new weekly releases, graphic novels, trading cards, and a curated pull-list service. McGinn is widely praised by regulars and visitors for his knowledge, his approachability, and his tendency to remember customers' reading preferences and names.

The longevity of Amazing Fantasy on Irving Street reflects a broader moment of commercial renewal in the Inner Sunset, where the SF New Deal Neighborhood Vibrancy Fund, the monthly Inner Sunset Flea Market, and a wave of new restaurants have injected fresh energy into the neighborhood's 9th Avenue and Irving Street corridors. The shop is open seven days a week at 650 Irving Street.

moreNews.headline: CASA Clubhouse Opens at Shirley Chisholm Village, Resolving Long-Running Community Room Dispute
moreNews.body: After more than a year of community frustration, the long-promised public meeting room beside Shirley Chisholm Village — the 135-unit affordable housing complex for SFUSD teachers near 43rd Avenue in the Outer Sunset — is now open. Children's After School Arts (CASA) signed a lease in April 2026 for the 1,562-square-foot space, which it now operates as the 'CASA Clubhouse.' A 749-square-foot community room within the space is available for public reservation. The room's extended vacancy had drawn vocal criticism from neighborhood residents, who had been promised access when the project was completed in April 2024. CASA has described the arrangement as combining its own programming offices and art space with broader neighborhood availability.

moreNews.headline: West Portal's Restaurant Boom Keeps Growing with New Cafés and Wine Bars
moreNews.body: West Portal Avenue has cemented its reputation as one of San Francisco's most surprising new dining destinations, with at least seven food and beverage businesses opening along the corridor in the past year alone. The most recent addition is Hardware Coffee Co., which opened in May 2026 in the former Papenhausen Hardware space at 32 West Portal Ave, operating as an all-day café with coffee, beer, wine, and a full-service florist. Other recent arrivals include Tur, a brunch spot from the team behind Khao Tiew; Binu Bonu, a wine bar from the original owners of La Ciccia in Noe Valley; and George's Donuts and Merriment. The SF Standard noted in June that West Portal has transformed into a culinary destination, attracting diners from across the city.

moreNews.headline: Affordable Senior Housing Project at 1234 Great Highway Remains on Hiatus
moreNews.body: The proposed 199-unit affordable senior housing development at 1234 Great Highway — slated to replace a Motel 6 and become the tallest building in the Outer Sunset — remains on an indefinite hold after its developers announced financing challenges in January 2026. Tenderloin Neighborhood Development Corporation and Self Help for the Elderly said they plan to reapply for funding in 2027 and, if successful, hope to begin construction in early 2028. The project had drawn intense neighborhood opposition despite its focus on housing seniors, a population that represents the fastest-growing segment of California's homeless population according to a 2024 UCSF report.

restaurants.name: Kothai Republic

restaurants.name: Caché

restaurants.name: Savor
restaurants.description: Entirely vegetarian Arabic café on Irving Street run by Chef Mohamed Aboghanem, beloved for flavorful mezze, hummus samplers, and a warm neighborhood atmosphere.

restaurants.name: Inle Burmese Cuisine

restaurants.name: Mezze and Mooore II

restaurants.name: The Little Shamrock

restaurants.name: Snowbird Coffee

restaurants.name: Binu Bonu

restaurants.name: Tur

shops.description: Inner Sunset comic book institution at 650 Irving Street, open since 1978 (under current owner Frank McGinn since 2000), offering new releases, back issues, graphic novels, and trading cards.

shops.name: General Store

shops.name: Case for Making

shops.description: Outer Sunset art supply store on Judah Street selling handmade watercolors, brushes, and specialty art materials, with hands-on workshops for all skill levels.

shops.name: The Last Straw
shops.description: Charming Outer Sunset storefront on Irving Street selling jewelry, clothing, and handbags in a bright and welcoming neighborhood shop.

shops.name: Sunset Mercantile Emporium

artEntertainment.address: Sloat Blvd & Great Hwy, San Francisco, CA 94132
